title: Alphonsus Liguori (1696–1787)
hook: a lawyer turned priest who taught moral theology with mercy

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jansenism, a strict movement that made communion feel like a prize for the nearly perfect. Your line was not a reward. Today, a man who fought that strictness from the confessional.

Lawyers are trained to read every line. Tradition says one young lawyer in Naples, quick, well trained and from a noble family, missed one detail in a document and lost an important case because of it. Tradition says he walked out of court, stayed shut away for days, and afterward left the law for good. Not long after, he gave up his sword at a shrine of Our Lady and set out to become a priest: a lawyer who had just learned how it feels to be wrong in public. His name is Alphonsus Liguori.
screen: `A LAWYER IN NAPLES.` → `ONE OVERLOOKED DETAIL.` → `HE LEAVES THE LAW.`

segments.voice: First, the countryside. As a priest, Alphonsus went out to the poor villages and goatherds in the hills around Naples, people he felt the Church had left behind. To preach to them he founded a congregation of priests and brothers named for the Most Holy Redeemer, today called the Redemptorists. Second, two ditches. Hearing confessions, he met two kinds of priest. Some were so strict that people left without absolution and stopped coming back. Others excused nearly everything. Neither, he thought, actually helped a person get free. Third, the book. So the former lawyer studied the cases. He wrote a long work of moral theology, weighing hard questions one by one, looking for the path between harshness and excuses. Where a law was truly in doubt, he argued, a person should not always be bound to the strictest answer. A confessor, he taught, is a father and a physician as well as a judge. Fourth, mercy with a spine. Mercy for Alphonsus never meant pretending sin isn't real. It meant judging the way God judges. In Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful." And straight after: "Judge not, and you shall not be judged." The Church later named Alphonsus a Doctor of the Church. He also wrote simple prayer books for ordinary people, and songs they could sing.
screen: `PREACHING TO THE FORGOTTEN POOR.` · `TOO HARSH, OR TOO LOOSE.` · `A LAWYER STUDIES THE CASES.` · `MERCY THAT STILL TELLS THE TRUTH.` · then, large: `BE YE THEREFORE MERCIFUL, AS YOUR FATHER ALSO IS MERCIFUL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you judged recently, out loud or in your head, and become their lawyer for a minute, the way Alphonsus studied his cases: what don't you know about their day, and what might they be carrying? You're not excusing anything, just letting the whole case into the room. If you pray, hold them before God by name; if not, simply wish them well.
Alphonsus Liguori. A Naples lawyer turned priest, founder of the Redemptorists, who taught confessors to judge with mercy.
Your line: mercy in judging. For Alphonsus, mercy never stopped telling the truth. Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Redemptorist priests and brothers still preach parish missions and hear confessions, and Catholic seminarians and confessors often study Alphonsus's moral theology; his short prayer books, like his visits to the Blessed Sacrament, are still prayed.

fork.setup: you're a confessor in Naples. a tired mother confesses the same sin she confessed last month. what do you do?
options: send her away without absolution until she proves she's changed.
welcome her kindly, absolve her and give her one small next step.
tell her it isn't really a sin, so she can stop worrying.
fork.reveal: Alphonsus rejected both ditches: harshness that drives people off, and excuses that leave them stuck. a confessor, he taught, is a father and a physician as well as a judge.

chat.says: Was Alphonsus Liguori soft on sin, since he pushed confessors toward mercy?
options: No. Mercy for him never meant pretending sin isn't real; it meant judging as God does.
Yes. He taught that confessors should excuse nearly everything they hear.
No. He actually wanted confessors to be stricter, to keep people from sin.

notes: The lost lawsuit (overlooked detail in a document) and his withdrawal afterward are given as tradition; confirm. 'Gave up his sword at a shrine of Our Lady' refers to his laying his sword at the altar of Our Lady of Ransom (Santa Maria della Mercede); confirm or cut.
'Goatherds in the hills around Naples' reflects the founding story at Scala; confirm.
His position on doubtful law (equiprobabilism) is simplified as 'a person should not always be bound to the strictest answer'; confirm the simplification is fair.
Confessor as father, physician, teacher and judge: Praxis Confessarii; the script names father, physician and judge. Confirm.
Doctor of the Church: stated without date. Patronage of confessors and moral theologians omitted under the claims rule.
'Songs they could sing' alludes to hymns such as Tu scendi dalle stelle; confirm.
